fieldMarks: Large, slim, gray-brown lizard with keeled scales, short legs and a tail about twice the body length; up to 5.6 in snout-vent (WDFW).
Brown back with black spots in transverse bands; fold of small scales along each side (WDFW).
Yellow or gold eyes; underside light with no dark pigment on the lateral edges of the scales (WDFW).
Juveniles have a plain brownish to reddish back and scales lighter than the body folds (WDFW).
behavior: Active by day and much less secretive than the northern alligator lizard; climbs shrubs and lower trunks with its prehensile tail and swims and basks on creek rocks (WDFW).
Bites when captured; tail is easily shed (WDFW).
Eats slugs, insects, centipedes, scorpions and spiders, plus lizards, small mammals and occasionally bird eggs and nestlings (NatureServe).
Lays 1-3 clutches of usually 5-20 eggs May-July; inactive in the coldest weather but active over a wide temperature range (NatureServe).
habitat: Grassland, chaparral, oak woodland and open pine forest; in drier regions along streams and other moist, vegetated areas; also logs, thickets, rocks and old woodpiles around houses (NatureServe; WDFW).
range: Mainly west of the Cascade-Sierra Nevada crest from south-central Washington through western Oregon and California to northern Baja California; introduced at Las Vegas, Nevada (NatureServe).

lookalikes.name: Northern alligator lizard
lookalikes.howToTell: Smaller (under 3.9 in snout-vent), brown eyes, dark pigment on the lateral edges of the belly scales (WDFW).
